# The problem and how we measure {#sec-problem}

**Every result in this book is a measurement of one mapping, from a
discretized boundary and a few global conditions to the steady field that
boundary induces, under one recipe, with one metric.** This chapter defines
the mapping and its general interface on an example whose exact solution we
know. It names the directions in which a learned operator must generalize.
It defines the metric and the instrument the metric is read on. The
datasets, their splits and the comparison protocol are in @sec-baselines.
After this chapter and that one, a reader who knows PDEs and transformers
but has never seen this program can read any later table.

```{python}
#| label: setup-problem
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection
from matplotlib.colors import Normalize
import json
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
J = lambda p: json.load(open(RES / p))
```

## The boundary-to-field problem {#sec-pde-theory}

**The object to learn is a solution operator, not a time stepper, and its
interface is the same for every steady boundary-driven problem.** The input
has three parts.

- **Boundary cells.** A closed boundary surface (in two dimensions, a closed
  curve) given as a mesh of cells, each carrying its position $x_i$, its
  outward unit normal $n_i$ and its measure $w_i$ (area in three dimensions,
  length in two). A cell can also carry **per-cell boundary scalars**, the
  data its boundary condition prescribes (a wall temperature, a prescribed
  flux). This channel is optional, and none of the benchmark datasets uses
  it.
- **$K$ global vector inputs.** Directions that belong to the problem rather
  than to any cell: a gravity or body-force direction, an applied field, the
  far-field flow direction. Each enters as a unit vector $\hat g_k$. A
  magnitude that matters is passed as one of the scalars below.
- **$S$ global scalar inputs.** The parameters of the PDE and of its
  far-field data: a diffusivity, a Young's modulus, a Reynolds number, a
  far-field speed.

The output is the steady field this data induces: pressure and wall shear
on the boundary itself, and pressure, velocity or other fields at arbitrary
**interior** points. Throughout the book *interior* means the domain the
boundary bounds. For a body in a stream, that is the fluid outside the
body. Interior query points carry no data. They are bare coordinates at
which the field is requested. There is no volume mesh, no initial state,
and nothing to advance in time.

**External aerodynamics is the benchmark instance of this interface.** It
has one closed body in a uniform far field and exactly one global direction
($K = 1$, the far-field direction). The car and wing datasets have no global
scalar ($S = 0$), because every case shares one far-field speed. The airfoil
dataset has one ($S = 1$), because the far-field speed varies from case to
case. The datasets are introduced in @sec-datasets. Nothing in the
architectures compared here is specific to that instance. The mechanism
chapters speak of "along a global direction", and gravity or an applied
field fits that phrase as well as a stream does.

@fig-problem-schematic draws the mapping on the simplest member of the
class, ideal flow around a lifting Joukowski airfoil. That flow has a
closed-form solution and is the running example of this book.

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-schematic
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The mapping this book studies, on the running example (ideal flow
#|   around a lifting Joukowski airfoil at 6° incidence, exact closed form).
#|   Left, the input: boundary cells with their outward normals (gray) and
#|   measures, plus the one global vector input this instance has, the unit
#|   far-field direction. Right, the output: the surface pressure
#|   coefficient along the boundary and the interior pressure field in the
#|   fluid outside the airfoil, requested at bare query points (black dots).
#|   How to read this: the figure shows what enters and what is scored; it
#|   does not show any model's prediction, and the industrial datasets are
#|   three-dimensional, turbulent and separated, where no closed form exists.
#| code-fold: true
Jk = joukowski(alpha_deg=6.0, n_cells=60)
xy, mid, nrm, cp_s, alpha = Jk["xy"], Jk["mid"], Jk["nrm"], Jk["cp_s"], Jk["alpha"]
# Interior field on a polar grid in the circle plane, mapped forward.
c = complex(-0.08, 0.08); a = abs(1.0 - c)
r = np.linspace(1.0 + 1e-3, 4.0, 90); th = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 241)
R_, T_ = np.meshgrid(r, th)
zeta_g = c + a * R_ * np.exp(1j * T_); z_g = zeta_g + 1 / zeta_g
cp_g = Jk["cp_field"](z_g)

fig, (axl, axr) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.4, 3.8))
for ax in (axl, axr):
    clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.6, 2.6); ax.set_ylim(-1.6, 1.8)
axl.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=INK, lw=1.8)
sel = slice(0, None, 3)
axl.quiver(mid[sel, 0], mid[sel, 1], nrm[sel, 0], nrm[sel, 1], color=MUTED, scale=9, width=0.004, headwidth=4)
axl.plot(mid[sel, 0], mid[sel, 1], "o", ms=3, color=INK)
axl.annotate("", xy=(-1.9 + 0.9 * np.cos(alpha), 1.3 + 0.9 * np.sin(alpha)), xytext=(-1.9, 1.3),
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=1.8))
axl.text(-2.4, 1.55, r"global vector input: unit far-field direction $\hat g_1$", color=INK2, fontsize=9)
axl.text(0.5, -0.08, "boundary cells: position $x_i$, normal $n_i$, measure $w_i$", color=INK2, fontsize=8.5,
         ha="center", transform=axl.transAxes)
axl.set_title("input")
lim = 1.6; norm = Normalize(-lim, 1.0)
axr.pcolormesh(z_g.real, z_g.imag, np.clip(cp_g, -lim, 1.0), cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm, shading="gouraud",
               alpha=0.85, rasterized=True)
segs = np.stack([xy[:-1], xy[1:]], axis=1)
axr.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=DIVERGING(norm(np.clip(cp_s, -lim, 1))), linewidths=4.5,
                                  capstyle="round", zorder=4))
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
rq = 1.0 + 1.6 * rng.random(70) ** 0.8; tq = 2 * np.pi * rng.random(70)
zq = c + a * rq * np.exp(1j * tq); zq = zq + 1 / zq
axr.plot(zq.real, zq.imag, ".", color=INK, ms=4, zorder=5)
axr.text(0.5, -0.08, "surface field on the boundary;\ninterior field at bare query points", color=INK2,
         fontsize=8.5, ha="center", va="top", transform=axr.transAxes)
axr.set_title("output")
sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm)
cb = fig.colorbar(sm, ax=axr, fraction=0.035, pad=0.02)
cb.set_label("pressure coefficient $C_p$ [–]", fontsize=9); cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
fig.text(0.49, 0.52, r"$\longmapsto$", fontsize=22, ha="center", va="center", color=INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=3.0)
plt.show()
```

**Why steady, boundary-driven problems.** The admitted class is steady,
well-posed, free of interior sources, and governed by the same equations
everywhere in the domain. For such problems the boundary data and the
global conditions determine the whole field, so a surrogate that consumes
only the boundary throws nothing away: the boundary *is* the problem. The
industrial targets are time-averaged turbulent flows around vehicles,
wings and airfoils. Their governing equations are not given to the model.
They are not even perfectly knowable, because the turbulence closure is an
empirical fit. Every claim about an architecture is therefore a measurement
against CFD labels, never against a closed form.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What potential theory says a correct boundary-to-field map must respect"}
For a harmonic field $u$ in a domain $\Omega$ with boundary $\Gamma$,
Green's third identity represents the interior value as a boundary integral,

$$
u(x)=\int_{\Gamma}\Bigl[G(x,y)\,\partial_{n_y}u(y)-u(y)\,\partial_{n_y}G(x,y)\Bigr]\,dS_y ,
$$ {#eq-green}

with $G$ the free-space fundamental solution, $n_y$ the outward normal at
the boundary point $y$ and $dS_y$ the boundary measure. The flows of
interest are separated and turbulent, far from harmonic, so the identity is
not a model. But it says what any correct map must respect, and three
consequences shape the architectures compared in this book.

1. **All-to-all coupling.** The density of the representation depends on
   the whole domain, not on $x - y$ and $n_y$ alone: every boundary patch
   influences every interior point, with no cutoff radius that survives a
   change of geometry.
2. **Integrals against boundary measure.** Both terms weight each cell by
   its area, so splitting one cell into two halves leaves the operator
   unchanged. This is why every dataset hands the model cell areas alongside
   positions and normals, and why ISLA's sums are quadrature rules
   (@sec-isla-quadrature).
3. **Exactly the shared symmetry, no more.** The map's symmetry is the
   symmetry shared by the equations, their coefficients, the boundary data
   and the nondimensional parameters. Homogeneity and constant coefficients
   buy translation invariance only. Anisotropic diffusion is not isotropic,
   and the screened Laplace equation $\Delta u - \kappa^2 u = 0$ is not scale
   invariant. Consider incompressible Navier–Stokes at fixed Reynolds number
   with a free-space far field and one distinguished global direction. That
   operator commutes with rigid motions and reflections. Once lengths are
   measured in a unit carried with the geometry, it also commutes with
   positive scalings. The map can then depend on the geometry only through
   the joint invariants of $\{x - y,\ n_y,\ \hat g_1\}$, which are
   magnitudes and pairwise angles. Dimensionless scalars can modulate
   everything freely, because a scalar breaks no symmetry. A ground plane, a
   second inlet or a Reynolds number that varies with size removes the
   corresponding symmetry. Each is therefore a property of a dataset rather
   than of the equations.

Which of these an architecture enforces by construction and which it learns
from data is the subject of @sec-isla (ISLA) and @sec-baselines
(GeoTransolver and Transolver). None of the three requires knowing the PDE.
:::

### What varies within a dataset {#sec-parametric}

**A dataset is a family of cases, and what the model must learn is fixed by
which parts of the interface vary across the family.** When only the
geometry varies, the global inputs are constants and the operator is
learned as a function of shape alone. When a global direction varies, the
model must represent how the field depends on it. When a global scalar
varies, it must represent how the field depends on a parameter of the
physics. The three benchmark datasets (@sec-datasets) span the three cases.
On DrivAerML only the geometry varies, and every car sits in the same far
field. On HiLiftAeroML each wing geometry is simulated across a range of
far-field directions, from attached flow through stall, so $\hat g_1$
changes from case to case. On AirfRANS the direction and the far-field
speed both vary, and the speed enters as the one global scalar. Coordinates
enter only in nondimensional form, scaled by the dataset's reference
length, so learned weights never see units. No architecture is told how the
field depends on any global input. Because HiLiftAeroML is a full
geometry-by-direction grid, its axes of variation can each be held out
separately (@sec-splits).

### What generalization means here

**A learned operator earns the name only if it behaves like an operator
away from its training distribution, and "away" has several independent
directions, each read by its own split or probe.** Six are named, one
question per split, never two combined into one score:

- **Data efficiency**: accuracy against the number of training cases on a
  fixed validation set (@sec-data-efficiency).
- **Regime extrapolation**: training on one flow regime (attached flow) and
  testing on another (post-stall), on a sealed test set evaluated once
  (@sec-limits-regime).
- **Unseen geometry**: validation geometries that never appear in training
  at any condition, as distinct from geometries seen at other conditions
  (@sec-splits).
- **Cross-family transfer**: zero-shot evaluation on a vehicle family
  different from the training family. The dataset for it is
  @sec-shift-suv, and the axis is unmeasured for ISLA
  (@sec-limits-transfer).
- **Pose**: the same cases presented in arbitrary rigid poses (@sec-pose).
  The physics does not depend on where the body sits in the laboratory, so
  the answer must not either.
- **Discretization**: the same cases presented under a different sampling
  draw at inference (@sec-sampling-laws), and, separately, a model trained
  under a different sampling law and scored on the original draw
  (@sec-training-law). The physics does not depend on how the surface was
  sampled, so the answer must not either.

The last two are the invariances ISLA is built for. @sec-invariances
defines them and their instruments.

## How we measure {#sec-part-eval}

**Every number in the book is one of a small set of quantities defined
here, each read on a stated instrument:** a relative field error, a
force-coefficient error, a paired per-case statistic, a seed-disagreement
statistic, a regime-extrapolation ratio, or an exact contract test.

### Field error, forces and paired statistics {#sec-metrics}

**The metric is the area-weighted relative L2 error of a field over the
sampled cells of one case, averaged over the validation cases, and it is
read in float32.** It scores error *per unit surface area*, so a large,
smooth cell of an open surface counts for more than the many small cells
packed into a slot or a corner. A per-point root-mean-square over the same
samples weights every cell equally and depends on where the mesher put its
cells. @tbl-metric-illustration shows the difference on the airfoil. One
prediction error is scored under two samplings of the same surface. It
gives the same area-weighted number and two different per-point numbers.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-metric-illustration
#| output: asis
# One synthetic prediction error, scored under two samplings of the running airfoil.
u = np.linspace(0, 1, 2001)
density = 1.0 + 14.0 * np.exp(-((u - 0.5) / 0.05) ** 2) + 2.0 * np.exp(-((u - 0.0) / 0.04) ** 2) + 2.0 * np.exp(-((u - 1.0) / 0.04) ** 2)
cdf = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(density[:-1] * np.diff(u))]); cdf /= cdf[-1]
Ju = joukowski(n_cells=60); Jm = joukowski(n_cells=60, frac=np.interp(np.linspace(0, 1, 61), cdf, u))
def err_field(JJ):
    # a smooth error concentrated near the leading edge (where the clustered sampler puts its cells)
    s = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(JJ["w"])]); sm = (s[:-1] + s[1:]) / 2 / s[-1]
    return 0.35 * np.exp(-((sm - 0.5) / 0.08) ** 2)
def rel_l2(JJ, w):
    e = err_field(JJ); w = w / w.sum()
    return np.sqrt(np.sum(w * e**2)) / np.sqrt(np.sum(w * JJ["cp_s"] ** 2))
out = "| sampling of the same airfoil | area-weighted relative L2 (the book's metric) | per-point relative L2 |\n|---|---:|---:|\n"
for JJ, lab in ((Ju, "equal-arclength cells"), (Jm, "cells clustered at the leading edge")):
    out += f"| {lab} | {rel_l2(JJ, JJ['w']):.3f} | {rel_l2(JJ, np.ones(len(JJ['w']))):.3f} |\n"
print(out)
print(": One prediction error, a smooth bump of amplitude 0.35 in the pressure coefficient centered on the "
      "leading edge, scored against the exact Joukowski solution under two samplings of the same surface "
      "with 60 cells each. The area-weighted relative L2 agrees between the samplings to quadrature error; "
      "the per-point relative L2 rises when the mesher places more cells where the error is. "
      "How to read this: the metric measures the field, not the mesh. It is a constructed illustration, not "
      "a measurement of any model. {#tbl-metric-illustration}")
```

For one case with sampled cells $j = 1,\dots,N$, prediction $\hat f_j$,
label $f_j$ and cell measures $w_j$ normalized to sum to one, the recipe
computes

$$
\varepsilon \equiv \frac{\sqrt{\sum_j w_j\,\lVert\hat f_j-f_j\rVert^2}}
{\sqrt{\sum_j w_j\,\lVert f_j\rVert^2}},
$$ {#eq-rel-l2}

where $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ is the vector norm for vector fields (velocity,
wall shear) and the absolute value for scalars. In the interior the weights
are cell volumes. The fields enter as the training pipeline presents them,
each shifted and scaled by dataset statistics. The denominator is therefore
the norm of the standardized label, and absolute values are comparable only
within one dataset and one pipeline. The quantity that carries across is
the *ratio* between two models scored on the same cases. **Every
cross-architecture ratio in the book is the named baseline's error divided
by ISLA's error on the same cases, so a ratio above one favors ISLA.**
This convention is stated here once and not restated per table.

**The reporting instrument is float32 inference on the final-epoch
checkpoint.** Training runs in bfloat16 (@sec-protocol). Scoring in
bfloat16 adds an architecture-dependent offset of several percent to the
mean error. The offset is larger for GeoTransolver and Transolver than for
ISLA, so a bfloat16 comparison flatters ISLA. Every bfloat16 number in the
book is labeled as such (@sec-protocol).

**A field error on the sampled cells is not a statement about an
integrated load.** Every model is scored on the same cells, so the field
comparison is fair; the integral of a signed field over a sample is not,
because drag and lift are integrals with heavy cancellation. On the
DrivAerML Surface task, with the reference checkpoints scored at the
reporting protocol:

```{python}
#| label: para-force-limit
#| output: asis
FR = J("forceref_2026-09-26.json")["summary"]
sm = lambda m, c, k: FR["models"][m][c]["seed_mean"][k]
print(f"- the 200,000-cell sample alone misses the full-surface drag by {100 * FR['sampling']['CD']['rel_l1_sampled_vs_full']:.1f}% "
      f"and the lift by {100 * FR['sampling']['CL']['rel_l1_sampled_vs_full']:.0f}%;\n"
      f"- against the sampled cells both architectures predict drag to within "
      f"{100 * max(sm('ISLA', 'CD', 'rel_l1_vs_sampled'), sm('GeoTransolver-512', 'CD', 'rel_l1_vs_sampled')):.1f}%;\n"
      f"- against the full surface their drag errors are {100 * sm('ISLA', 'CD', 'rel_l1_vs_full'):.2f}% (ISLA) and "
      f"{100 * sm('GeoTransolver-512', 'CD', 'rel_l1_vs_full'):.2f}% (GeoTransolver-512).\n\n"
      "A force claim therefore needs the full surface at inference or a stated sampling band. One dataset. "
      "Data: results/forceref_2026-09-26.json.")
```

```{python}
#| label: para-metric-calibration
#| output: asis
# parameter-free reference predictors on the 180 shared HiLiftAeroML validation cases; the far-field-relative scale
ref = J("hilift_reference_predictors_35_2026-09-06.json")["summary"]
print(f"**What a relative L2 value means, calibrated on HiLiftAeroML.** On the far-field-relative pressure scale "
      f"($p - p_\\infty$, so the error is normalized by the pressure variation over the surface rather than by its absolute level; "
      f"geometric mean over the 180 shared validation cases; not the recipe metric), predicting the far-field pressure everywhere "
      f"scores exactly {ref['const_p_inf_rel_l2_gmean']:.2f} by construction, the dataset-mean pressure {ref['const_dataset_mean_rel_l2_gmean']:.2f}, "
      f"and each case's own mean pressure {ref['const_case_mean_rel_l2_gmean']:.2f}. A model knows something about a case only when it "
      f"beats the last of these. The trained architectures on the recipe metric are in @sec-surface. "
      f"Data: results/hilift_reference_predictors_35_2026-09-06.json (constants only).")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The other quantities: forces, paired statistics, seed disagreement, regime ratio"}
**Force coefficients.** Inference integrates predicted pressure and wall
shear into drag and lift coefficients per case (reference area one) and
integrates the CFD labels on the *same* 200,000 sampled cells to form the
reference. The reported error is the mean absolute coefficient error over
the validation cases divided by the mean magnitude of the reference
coefficient, averaged over seeds. It is an error against the sampled-cell
label integral, not the full-surface force: the shared quadrature cancels
the sampling error common to prediction and label.

**Paired per-case statistics.** Because every architecture is scored on the
same 180 HiLiftAeroML cases (or 48 DrivAerML cars), each case yields one
paired comparison of the architectures' seed-mean errors. Three statistics
are reported. The first is the number of cases on which ISLA has the lower
seed-mean error, with the exact two-sided sign test. The second is the
stricter count of cases on which ISLA wins on every seed. The third is the
median and the 10th to 90th percentile of the per-case error ratio.

**Seed disagreement.** With two independently seeded models of one
architecture, the per-case relative L2 of one seed's prediction against the
other's is the cheapest uncertainty estimate available. Its Spearman rank
correlation with the per-case error against the truth measures whether the
model knows where it is wrong (@sec-data-efficiency).

**Regime-extrapolation ratio.** On the sealed angle-of-attack and stall
splits the readout is $d \equiv \varepsilon_{\text{test}} /
\varepsilon_{\text{val}}$, the out-of-regime error divided by the same
model's in-regime validation error. It is always reported beside the
absolute test error, because a smaller $d$ can also come from a higher
in-regime floor (@sec-limits-regime).

**The far-field-relative scale** ($p - p_\infty$) of the calibration
paragraph above and of the seed-disagreement analysis is $\lVert\hat p -
p\rVert / \lVert p - p_\infty\rVert$ with the geometric mean over cases.
Numbers on the two scales are not interchangeable. Per-case ratios between
two models coincide on both, because the numerators are the same.
Case-averaged values do not.
:::

### Contracts are exact tests, not metrics {#sec-fidelity-columns}

**A structural property an architecture claims is asserted to roundoff in
float64 as a unit test, never averaged into a score.** A contract is a
statement such as "a rigidly moved input produces the rigidly moved
output". It either holds to roundoff on random weights and a random point
cloud or it is not claimed. It is therefore a property of the code rather
than of any trained checkpoint. That is what makes it worth more than a
small measured degradation: it holds for every input, including the ones no
validation set contains. What the float64 test certifies is the algebraic
construction. The residual on the trained GPU path is a separate measured
quantity, small in float32 and several percent in bfloat16
(@sec-isla-contracts). The contracts ISLA holds, and the tests that
verify each, are tabulated in @sec-isla-contracts.

A property that is *not* enforced by construction, GeoTransolver's pose
behavior for instance, is measured as an accuracy degradation under
transformed inputs and reported as a number (@sec-pose, @sec-pose-contract),
never as a pass. The same distinction runs through @sec-invariances: of the
two invariances ISLA is built for, one is a contract and the other an
acceptance criterion read from a convergence measurement.
